A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same patch-level training work. All pages, equations, tables, and figures are readable. v2 ends with references; v3 adds Appendices A–D. The title change and additions do not prevent reliable comparison.

before.justification: Section 3 reports original language-model training results, downstream evaluations, scaling experiments, and ablations.

after.justification: v3 retains the original experiments and adds throughput measurements, a mixup comparison, and tokenizer experiments in its appendices.

M1.justification: The main method retains consecutive-token embedding averaging, single-head next-patch prediction, and subsequent token-level training. Appendix C introduces an experimental mixup variant that instead groups corresponding tokens from randomly selected training samples. This is a limited alternative aggregation procedure; the new pseudocode and projection terminology clarify the existing main method.

E1.justification: Training and evaluation retain the Pile, WikiText-103, six zero-shot benchmarks, Alpaca instruction tuning, and MT-Bench. Appendix D changes tokenization of the existing data, without adding a dataset, domain, or task. Mixup changes the training procedure rather than coverage.

E2.justification: Figure 9 adds Mixup K=4 as a comparator alongside patch-level initialization and training without initialization. Existing comparator sets remain. Table 5's InputMap/OutputMap become InputProj/OutputProj with identical results, so these are renamed comparators.

E3.justification: Tables 3–4 switch the reported scaling metric from perplexity to cross-entropy loss. New supplementary protocols include throughput comparisons with gradient accumulation adjusted to preserve batch size, and LLaMA3 tokenization with a 128,000-word vocabulary, approximately 300B training tokens, and a 75B-token patch-size study. The original main experimental settings are retained.

E4.justification: Appendices B–D substantially extend the supplementary analyses: measured throughput tests practical efficiency and synchronization overhead; mixup tests whether consecutive-token grouping matters; and tokenizer experiments test sensitivity to compression rate, including K=2 versus K=4. These address practical validity and design choices beyond the retained scaling, architecture, patch-size, and activation analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance-testing procedures. The added experiments retain point estimates and single displayed trajectories.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial empirical evidence. Table 6 reports 247.1K baseline tokens/second versus 933.5K and 864.2K for two patch configurations, yielding 3.78× and 3.50× speedups. Under the new LLaMA3-tokenizer setting, Table 7 reports baseline/patch perplexities of 15.48/15.32 and average accuracies of 42.8/42.9. Figures 9–11 add mixup and tokenizer findings. Tables 1, 2, and 5 retain their values; Tables 3–4 express existing scaling results as log losses, not improved performance.

T1.justification: The compute relationship, patch-embedding definition, and training objective remain mathematically equivalent; changing pθ to P is notation. Appendix B substitutes measured speed into the existing cost accounting. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contribution and claim: patch-level training followed by token-level adaptation approximately halves training compute while maintaining performance for 370M–2.7B models. The expanded title and additional supporting experiments do not redefine that claim.

C2.justification: Sections 2 and 3.7 newly interpret an unchanged input or output interface as an anchor for representation transfer. Appendix B qualifies theoretical savings with data-loading and synchronization overhead. Appendix D adds the interpretation that tokenizer compression affects suitable patch size. Appendix C connects its new control to the existing long-range-dependency hypothesis.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds implementation pseudocode for embedding aggregation, position IDs, shifted labels/logits, and loss averaging. Appendix B supplies eight-A100 hardware and local batch, block-length, and accumulation settings for its measurements. Appendix D documents tokenizer-specific configurations. These supplement the already detailed setup; the source-code access information is unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds Shao et al. (2019, 2020, 2023) to the non-autoregressive training-objective discussion, plus Dubey et al. (2024) and Zhang et al. (2018) for LLaMA3 and mixup. The positioning relative to model growth, multi-token prediction, and patch-level models remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The title gains 'Beyond Next Token Prediction,' conference-publication headers replace 'Preprint,' and several method and interpretation paragraphs receive local edits. Appendices A–D extend the document, while the main section order and most prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds a substantial supplementary display set: throughput Table 6, tokenizer comparison Table 7, loss-trajectory Figures 9–11, and a boxed pseudocode listing. Existing Figures 1–8 remain, while Tables 3–4 receive metric-caption changes and Table 5 receives renamed labels. The expansion adds new visual evidence without redesigning the main paper.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens practical credibility through measured throughput and an explicit distinction between theoretical 0.5× cost and approximately 0.523× estimated runtime in Appendix B. Mixup and tokenizer controls add useful validation, and pseudocode improves reproducibility. These are focused improvements to an already developed empirical paper: the main results remain unchanged, the added model-quality experiments concern 370M models, and uncertainty reporting is still absent.
